objectives.official_wording: Translate business problems into Claude-based AI solutions
objectives.module_reference: M1 How Claude Behaves, Decomposition; M2 Sizing (scoping, feasibility, verdicts, scoping-call case).

sections.What you need to know:
- **Start from the four properties of generative AI.** Each one is a capability, a limitation and a mitigation `[MODULE 1 – How Claude Behaves]`:
  - **Next-token prediction:** strong on common patterns, weak on precise specifics. Mitigate with citations, generator-verifier loops, tool lookups.
  - **Knowledge:** unreliable on rare or fast-changing topics. Mitigate with RAG, tools, MCP, web search.
  - **Working memory:** the context window is a hard edge. Mitigate with progressive loading and chunking.
  - **Steerability:** strong on concrete instructions, weak on abstract ones or precise maths. Mitigate with structured outputs and code execution.
- **Scoping sequence** `[MODULE 2 – Sizing]`: business requirement → capability list → architecture sketch (who owns each capability) → boundary conditions → SOW scope.
- **Feasibility verdict** `[MODULE 2]`: *feasible as scoped* · *feasible with constraints* · *not feasible*. A verdict comes with the constraints that make it true.
- **Constraints first:** gather volume, input size and latency before confirming feasibility. `[MODULE 2 – scoping call case]`
sections.Why it matters: Most expensive early mistake: over-assigning work to Claude. Confirming capability before collecting constraints leads to commitments the design can't keep. `[MODULE 1]` `[MODULE 2]`
sections.Architecture concepts: Capability inventory; ownership map (Claude / systems / humans); compensating controls per property; boundary conditions written into the SOW; cost model at production volume. `[MODULE 2]`
sections.How it works:
1. Run structured discovery and translate preferences into constraints (6.1).
2. Split the goal into named capabilities.
3. Assign each capability to Claude, an existing system or a human (1.5).
4. Run each capability through the four properties and add compensating controls.
5. Size cost and latency at production volume (2.4, 4.5).
6. Issue the verdict with explicit boundary conditions.
7. Put the boundary conditions into the SOW.
sections.Decision framework:
| Question | Guidance |
|---|---|
| When to give Claude the work | Language understanding, summarising, drafting, planning, tool-mediated actions |
| When NOT to | Authoritative values, live state, deterministic rules, high-stakes approvals |
| Alternatives | Existing systems of record; rules engines; human decision points |
| Trade-off | More given to Claude means faster to build but higher cost, more variance and more audit risk |
sections.Exam decision signals:
- "Excited sponsor, working demo, no volume numbers yet" → **gather constraints before the verdict**.
- "Needs exact amounts / IDs" → next-token limit → **verification or a tool lookup**.
- "Only works for short documents" → **feasible with constraints**; document the boundary.
sections.Common traps:
- COMMON TRAP: answering "can Claude do this?" and stopping there.
- COMMON TRAP: assigning deterministic routing to the model.
- COMMON TRAP: leaving "feasible with constraints" undocumented. It becomes infeasible the moment a constraint is violated in production.
sections.Must remember:
- Capability ≠ feasibility.
- Use the four properties as a lens on every capability.
- A verdict is the conclusion plus the constraints that make it true.
- Collect volume, input size and latency before committing.
sections.Quick recall:
**"Ask → Split → Assign → Stress-test (4 properties) → Size → Verdict."**

**Sources:** M1 How Claude Behaves, Decomposition; M2 Sizing (scoping, feasibility, verdicts, scoping-call case).

sections.What you need to know:
An end-to-end design has four stages. Each stage has an owner, a set of controls and a signal it emits. `[INFERENCE – assembled from the sources cited]`
| Stage | Design content | Source |
|---|---|---|
| **Input** | Identity injected by the server; data minimised to what the task needs; input screening (incl. retrieved and tool content) | `[MODULE 2]` `[MODULE 3]` |
| **Processing** | Pattern (augmented LLM / workflow / agent); reference architecture; model tier; context strategy; tools behind authorization | `[MODULE 1]` |
| **Output** | Output contract or schema; output screening; validation; confidence score; routing to a human by stakes | `[MODULE 1]` `[MODULE 3]` |
| **Feedback loop** | Outcome logging (accepted/rejected downstream); evals; drift detection; Signals → Triage → Decide → Act → Review; iterate vs. re-architect | `[MODULE 2]` `[MODULE 4]` |
`[OFFICIAL ANTHROPIC DOCS – Building effective agents]`: the augmented LLM (retrieval, tools, memory) is the basic building block. Start with the simplest solution and add complexity only when it's needed.
sections.Why it matters: A system without an outcome signal can't tell it's degrading. A system without an exception path pushes low-confidence work downstream at the same rate as clean work. `[MODULE 2]` `[MODULE 4]`
sections.Architecture concepts: Exception paths, human review queues, shared trace IDs, version pinning, governance tables (signal → trigger → owner → action). `[MODULE 1, 2, 4]`
sections.How it works:
1. Define the input contract and its identity and data controls.
2. Choose the processing pattern and reference architecture.
3. Define the output contract and the validation and screening steps.
4. Define confidence thresholds and the exception route.
5. Instrument outcome signals.
6. Wire signals into evals and a governance table before launch.
sections.Architecture example:
REAL-WORLD EXAMPLE – Invoice processing:
- **Input:** OCR plus server-side tenant ID.
- **Processing:** extraction against a schema, with an evaluator-optimizer pass.
- **Output:** schema-validated JSON; low-confidence fields go to a human queue.
- **Feedback:** reviewer corrections are logged and added to the golden dataset; a drop in eval score triggers an architect review. `[MODULE 1 – Doc pipeline]` `[MODULE 2]` `[MODULE 4]`
sections.Decision framework:
| Use a full four-stage design when… | A simpler design may do when… |
|---|---|
| Production, regulated or high-volume | Internal prototype with no downstream effects (still log outcomes) |
| Trade-off: more components to maintain, in exchange for detectability and recoverability | |
sections.Exam decision signals:
- "No exception path" → add confidence scoring and a human queue.
- "Quality slid for weeks unnoticed" → the feedback loop is missing.
- "Can't explain a decision afterwards" → decision logging.
sections.Common traps:
- COMMON TRAP: the diagram stops at "response to user".
- COMMON TRAP: monitoring without triggers (6.3).
- COMMON TRAP: one path for clean and messy inputs.
sections.Must remember:
- Every stage has controls and a signal.
- The feedback loop is part of the architecture.
- Exceptions need their own route.
- Simplest pattern first.
sections.Quick recall:
**"In (who/what) → Do (pattern) → Out (contract/check) → Learn (signal/loop)."**

**Sources:** M1 Reference Architectures; M2 Integration & Observability; M3 Guardrails; M4 Feedback loop; Official – Building effective agents.

objectives.official_wording: Select appropriate architectural patterns (workflow, agentic, augmented LLM)
objectives.module_reference: M1 Pattern Selection, 90-day retrospective, Key takeaways; Official – Building effective agents.
source_labels: OFFICIAL ANTHROPIC DOCS – Building effective agents

sections.What you need to know:
| Pattern | Control flow | Use when | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Augmented LLM** | One bounded call (may use tools, retrieval, thinking); no branching on model decisions | Well-defined task, verifiable output | `[MODULE 1]` |
| **Workflow** | Steps orchestrated **in your code** ("predefined code paths") | Steps knowable in advance; error cost real; observability matters | `[MODULE 1]` `[OFFICIAL ANTHROPIC DOCS]` |
| **Agent** | **The model** directs its own tool use | Path can't be enumerated in advance, *and* unexpected outputs are acceptable and recoverable | `[MODULE 1]` |

**Workflow sub-patterns** `[OFFICIAL ANTHROPIC DOCS – Building effective agents]`:
- **prompt chaining**, with programmatic gates between steps;
- **routing**, when categories are distinct and classification is accurate;
- **parallelization**, either *sectioning* or *voting*;
- **orchestrator-workers**, where subtasks are decided at runtime;
- **evaluator-optimizer**.

Combine them as needed; choose the simplest one that meets error tolerance and observability needs. `[MODULE 1]`

**Five factors, checked in order:** predictability → error cost → observability → latency → cost. The first factor that rules a pattern out decides; the tightest constraint picks the pattern. `[MODULE 1 – Key takeaways]`

**Agents in production** need limited tool entry points, per-turn budgets, explicit permissions and stopping criteria. `[MODULE 1]`

**Order of improvements:** better prompt → tools or retrieval → stronger pattern (e.g. evaluator-optimizer) → fine-tuning only for very high volume, critical latency, or format consistency that prompting couldn't fix. Fine-tuning availability is limited. `[MODULE 1]`
sections.Why it matters: Teams pick agents because a task *feels* open-ended. One team's traces showed only four paths. A router with four chains would have been auditable and cost six months less. `[MODULE 1 – 90-day retrospective]`
sections.Architecture concepts: Predictability vs. autonomy axes; agent liability surface; audit points (discrete steps); packaging as prompt only, direct tool use, or a Skill. `[MODULE 1]`
sections.How it works:
1. Can you write down the steps? Yes → workflow (or an augmented call if it's a single step).
2. Is a wrong output costly or hard to undo? Yes → a workflow with gates, or HITL.
3. Must an auditor point at a specific step? → workflow.
4. Do latency or cost budgets rule out multi-call loops? → augmented LLM.
5. Is the path truly unknowable *and* errors recoverable? → a bounded agent.
6. Revisit with production traces.
sections.Architecture example: REAL-WORLD EXAMPLE – A disbursement approval built as an agent couldn't answer "which step approved this?". Mining the traces found four shapes. A router with four chains gave discrete, auditable steps. `[MODULE 1]`
sections.Decision framework:
| Use workflow when… | Use agent when… |
|---|---|
| Paths are enumerable; compliance needs auditable steps | Open-ended investigation; next step depends on what was just found |
| **Avoid workflow** when you'd be scripting endless branches | **Avoid agent** when steps are knowable or an error can't be undone |
| Key clue: "auditor / approval step / known categories" | Key clue: "unfamiliar codebase / research across sources / can't predict steps" |
sections.Exam decision signals:
- "Four kinds of request" → **routing workflow**.
- "Draft then check quality" → **evaluator-optimizer**.
- "Independent sections in parallel" → **parallelization (sectioning)**.
- "Want flexibility for the future" → **trap**; build for the shape you know today.
sections.Common traps:
- COMMON TRAP: an agent as the "safe default".
- COMMON TRAP: fine-tuning before improving the prompt.
- COMMON TRAP: assuming agents always cost more. Accumulated context and call count drive cost, not the label. `[MODULE 1]`
sections.Must remember:
- Workflow = your code controls flow; agent = the model does.
- Use an agent only for genuinely unpredictable paths.
- Agents need budgets, limits and stopping criteria.
- Prompt → tools → stronger pattern → (rarely) fine-tune.
- Five factors; the tightest constraint picks the pattern.
sections.Quick recall:
**"Can you write the steps? Then write them."**

**Sources:** M1 Pattern Selection, 90-day retrospective, Key takeaways; Official – Building effective agents.

objectives.official_wording: Design multi-agent systems and orchestration strategies
objectives.module_reference: M1 Multi-agent systems, fan-out case; M2 Failure modes, least privilege; Official – multi-agent research system.
source_labels: OFFICIAL ANTHROPIC DOCS – multi-agent research system

sections.What you need to know:
- **Orchestrator:** owns the goal; decomposes, delegates and synthesises. It doesn't do sub-task work itself.
- **Subagents:** own scoped sub-tasks, each in its own context. `[MODULE 1]`
- **Three things to design, not assume:**
  - how the work is decomposed;
  - how each result is structured so it can be combined;
  - how conflicts and gaps are resolved. `[MODULE 1]`
- **Fan-out** is the common shape: split a large item into independent units, dispatch in parallel, synthesise. `[MODULE 1]`
- **Error recovery is asymmetric:**
  - subagent failure → usually recoverable (retry, re-route or flag);
  - orchestrator failure → often unrecoverable, so checkpoint its state;
  - make subagent work idempotent. `[MODULE 1]`
- **Coverage check at synthesis:** results returned must equal units dispatched. `[MODULE 1]`
- **HITL gates** go before irreversible or high-stakes subagent actions; sample the lower-stakes ones. `[MODULE 1]`
- `[OFFICIAL ANTHROPIC DOCS – multi-agent research system]` Multi-agent systems suit heavy parallelisation, information exceeding one context window, and many complex tools. They use about 15× the tokens of chat and fit poorly where all agents need shared context or have many dependencies.
sections.Why it matters: The most dangerous failure is a confident, complete-looking synthesis over incomplete work. In one case, "48 reviewed, 3 flagged" was reported when 50 sections were dispatched. `[MODULE 1]`
sections.Architecture concepts: Shared trace ID; result schema; conflict-resolution rule or human escalation; least-privilege tools per subagent `[MODULE 2]`; checkpointing; per-subagent budgets.
sections.How it works:
1. Confirm the work exceeds one context or benefits from parallel work.
2. Define units and an idempotent subagent contract (input and output schema).
3. Scope tools per subagent.
4. Dispatch; validate each result; retry or flag failures.
5. Reconcile coverage (returned = dispatched).
6. Resolve conflicts by rule or escalate.
7. Checkpoint orchestrator state and propagate the trace ID.
sections.Architecture example: REAL-WORLD EXAMPLE – Audit a 400-file codebase: one subagent per module with read-only tools, a findings schema, an orchestrator coverage check, a conflict rule (the stricter severity wins), and a human gate before any auto-fix PR. `[MODULE 1]` `[INFERENCE]`
sections.Decision framework:
| Use multi-agent when… | Use single agent / workflow when… |
|---|---|
| Work exceeds one context; independent units; breadth-first | Work fits in one context; heavy interdependence; tight budget |
| Trade-off: parallelism and clean contexts vs. many times the tokens and more failure boundaries | Use the fewest agents that meet the requirement |
sections.Exam decision signals:
- "Summary looked complete, units missing" → **coverage reconciliation**.
- "Run fails, all work lost" → **checkpoint the orchestrator**.
- "Can't trace across agents" → **shared trace ID**.
- "Subagent can delete prod" → scope tools; put a gate before irreversible actions.
sections.Common traps:
- COMMON TRAP: multi-agent as the default.
- COMMON TRAP: putting compliance-critical checks in subagents rather than deterministic code. `[MODULE 1 – bank case]`
- COMMON TRAP: no conflict-resolution rule.
sections.Must remember:
- The orchestrator delegates and synthesises.
- Subagent failure is recoverable; orchestrator failure often isn't.
- Reconcile coverage; never assume it.
- Fewest agents possible; a shared trace ID across them.
sections.Quick recall:
**"Split · Scope · Send · Check · Count · Combine."**

**Sources:** M1 Multi-agent systems, fan-out case; M2 Failure modes, least privilege; Official – multi-agent research system.

objectives.official_wording: Apply decomposition techniques for complex problem solving
objectives.module_reference: M1 Decomposition, fan-out, Assembly; M2 Scoping; Official – Building effective agents.
source_labels: OFFICIAL ANTHROPIC DOCS – Building effective agents

sections.What you need to know:
In the modules, decomposition works at three levels:
1. **Ownership decomposition:** Claude, existing systems or humans, justified by **reversibility, stakes and accountability**. This produces a *delegation map*: AI-appropriate, human-retained, or collaborative (Claude drafts, a person decides). `[MODULE 1 – Decomposition]`
2. **Capability decomposition:** split the business goal into named capabilities. `[MODULE 2 – Scoping]`
3. **Task / work decomposition:**
   - workflow steps or prompt chains with gates `[OFFICIAL ANTHROPIC DOCS – Building effective agents]`;
   - fan-out into independent units `[MODULE 1]`;
   - pipeline stages when inputs exceed the context window `[MODULE 2 – feasibility]`.

Delegation is the first of the four AI Fluency competencies. `[MODULE 1]`
sections.Why it matters: Over-assigning to Claude is the most common and most expensive early mistake. It makes the process more expensive, slower and harder to run. `[MODULE 1]`
sections.Architecture concepts: Delegation map, chain gates, unit independence (needed for parallelism), stage handoffs with narrow interfaces. `[MODULE 1]`
sections.How it works:
1. List the capabilities.
2. For each, ask: can a wrong call be undone? What does it cost? Who answers for it?
3. Assign to Claude, a system, a human or collaborative.
4. Break Claude's share into steps or units; add gates between steps.
5. Confirm the units are independent before running them in parallel.
6. Define the output schema for each step.
sections.Decision framework:
| Assign to Claude | To systems | To humans |
|---|---|---|
| Language, drafting, summarising, planning | Records, rules, live state | Approvals, exceptions, irreversible high-stakes calls |
| Collaborative where Claude drafts and the cost of a wrong call is high but recoverable with review | | |
sections.Exam decision signals:
- "Who should approve?" → reversibility, stakes, accountability.
- "Rules table already exists" → **keep it in the system**.
- "Document too long for the window" → **pipeline or chunked decomposition**.
sections.Common traps:
- COMMON TRAP: "Claude does everything".
- COMMON TRAP: parallelising dependent steps.
- COMMON TRAP: having no gate between chain steps.
sections.Must remember:
- Three owners: Claude, systems, humans.
- Reversibility, stakes, accountability.
- Decompose, then gate.
- Only independent units go in parallel.
sections.Quick recall:
**"R-S-A decides who owns it."**

**Sources:** M1 Decomposition, fan-out, Assembly; M2 Scoping; Official – Building effective agents.

objectives.official_wording: Align solutions to business value pillars (efficiency, transformation, productivity, cost, performance SLAs)
objectives.module_reference: M2 Business value and ROI mapping; M4 Outcome document; EG Domain 1 objective wording.
source_labels: MODULE 2 – Business value and ROI mapping

sections.What you need to know:
**Five pillars** `[EXAM GUIDE]` `[MODULE 2 – Business value and ROI mapping]`:
- **Efficiency:** the same work faster or cheaper.
- **Transformation:** work that wasn't feasible before.
- **Productivity:** more output from the same people.
- **Cost:** the run cost of the solution (M2 calls this "solution cost").
- **Performance SLAs:** service levels the deployment must hold.

**ROI mapping in four steps** `[MODULE 2]`:
1. Baseline measured in a business unit, using the owner's own data.
2. Projected state in the same unit, including human-review effort if the design has a review gate.
3. Subtract the run cost taken from the *sizing distribution* (not the average).
4. Payback period plus sensitivity analysis.

**Outcome document fields** `[MODULE 4]`: use case + scope boundary, metric before, metric after, the control that makes it auditable, measurement owner. (A sixth field, "reuse potential", is Partner-Track and optional.)
sections.Why it matters: A feasible design isn't automatically worth building. Technical metrics (volume, latency, error rate) show the system runs, not what it's worth. A CFO asks for the before-and-after on the business metric. `[MODULE 2]` `[MODULE 4]`
sections.Architecture concepts: The KPI translation layer `[MODULE 2]`; baseline capture at the start; SLA thresholds traced to their sources `[MODULE 4]`.
sections.How it works:
1. Tag each value claim with its pillar.
2. Capture the baseline before deployment.
3. Project in the same unit, net of review effort.
4. Subtract run cost from the sizing model.
5. State payback and its sensitivity.
6. Instrument the before-and-after metric and name its owner.
sections.Decision framework:
| Situation | Pillar emphasis |
|---|---|
| Same task, fewer hours | Efficiency / productivity |
| New capability (e.g. review 100% instead of a sample) | Transformation |
| Budget-constrained sponsor | Cost (tiering, caching, batch) |
| Customer-facing latency promise | Performance SLA (p95) |
sections.Exam decision signals:
- "CFO asks what it saved" → **before/after business metric + auditable control**.
- "Assumes full automation, but a human reviews" → **overstated value**.
- "Average token cost used" → **understated run cost**.
sections.Common traps:
- COMMON TRAP: an estimated (intuitive) baseline.
- COMMON TRAP: a metrics-only outcome document.
- COMMON TRAP: quoting payback without sensitivity.
sections.Must remember:
- Five pillars; tag every claim.
- Measure the baseline; don't guess it.
- Net out the review effort.
- Run cost comes from the sizing distribution.
- Before + after + control + owner.
sections.Quick recall:
**"E-T-P-C-S: Efficiency, Transformation, Productivity, Cost, SLA."**

**Sources:** M2 Business value and ROI mapping; M4 Outcome document; EG Domain 1 objective wording.

objectives.official_wording: Select appropriate Claude models based on trade-offs
objectives.module_reference: M1 Model selection, eval gate, Sonnet→Haiku case, Opus case, extended thinking; M2 Sizing, scoping-call case, version pinning.

sections.What you need to know:
**The tiers** (Opus, Sonnet, Haiku) trade capability against cost and latency. `[MODULE 1]`
- **Sonnet is the default** starting point.
- **Opus:** demanding reasoning, advanced coding, research synthesis, *when an eval shows Sonnet misses the bar*.
- **Haiku:** only when an eval confirms the quality trade-off is acceptable (e.g. classification, routing).

**Every model change is a release.** Gate it with `[MODULE 1]`:
- a curated, representative test set;
- a grading function;
- a **delta threshold set before running**.

**Use different tiers per step** where the evals support it. `[MODULE 1]`
**Context window capacity is part of the tier decision** (e.g. 1M vs. 200k tokens decides whether a 300-page contract needs chunking). `[MODULE 2]`
**Extended thinking:** adaptive thinking with an effort setting is the recommended control on current models. Thinking tokens are billed as output. Enable it only for a measured accuracy gap after prompt work. `[MODULE 1]` (Version specifics: verify.)
**Version pinning** plus monitoring the deprecations page. `[MODULE 2]`
A prompt tuned on one model is a starting point for another, not a finished artifact. `[MODULE 1]`
sections.Why it matters: "Not choosing a model is equivalent to choosing the most expensive one." One team defaulting to Opus everywhere ran at 7× the cost model; per-step tiering cut 71%. `[MODULE 1]`
sections.Architecture concepts: Model router per step; eval-gated migration; partial migration by input class; rollback criteria. `[MODULE 1]`
sections.How it works:
1. Start every step on Sonnet.
2. Build a per-step eval, stratified by input type.
3. Try one tier lower on easy steps and one higher on hard ones.
4. Accept only where per-category scores clear the pre-set floor.
5. Route by input class if only some classes pass.
6. Pin versions; re-validate on any update.
sections.Architecture example: REAL-WORLD EXAMPLE – A document pipeline moves to Haiku. Two document types fall below the 0.85 floor and stay on Sonnet through the existing classifier; the rest move to Haiku. Cost drops without the regression. `[MODULE 1]`
sections.Decision framework:
| Use Opus when… | Use Haiku when… |
|---|---|
| Eval shows a Sonnet gap on hard reasoning or synthesis | Eval shows acceptable quality on simple, high-volume steps |
| **Avoid** as a blanket default | **Avoid** on steps that fail per-category floors |
sections.Exam decision signals:
- "Use the best model to be safe" → **trap**.
- "Downgrade to save cost" → **eval with a pre-set floor, per category**.
- "Model version rolled forward" → **pin + re-validate**.
sections.Common traps:
- COMMON TRAP: judging a downgrade on the average score only.
- COMMON TRAP: setting the threshold after seeing the results.
- COMMON TRAP: "smallest model regardless of task fit" (EG Sample 2 distractor).
sections.Must remember:
- Sonnet default; move only on evidence.
- A model swap is a release.
- Thresholds are set in advance.
- Per-step and per-category decisions.
- Pin versions.
sections.Quick recall:
**"Start Sonnet · Prove the move · Pin the version."**

**Sources:** M1 Model selection, eval gate, Sonnet→Haiku case, Opus case, extended thinking; M2 Sizing, scoping-call case, version pinning.

objectives.official_wording: Design system prompts, templates, and guardrails
objectives.module_reference: M1 Prompting as Architecture, reusable prompt asset exercise; M3 Alignment layers.

sections.What you need to know:
An enterprise system prompt is a **designed asset** with structure: role and scope, constraints (must / must not), and an **output contract**. Ambiguity in a reused asset is a defect multiplied across every request. `[MODULE 1 – Prompting as Architecture]`
**Templates:** parameterised slots plus fixed scaffolding that carries the consistency and safety guarantees. Filling a slot can't remove a constraint, so *the safe path is the default path*. `[MODULE 1]`
**Description** (an AI Fluency competency): state scope, format and constraints explicitly. Underspecification is a gap the model fills differently each time. `[MODULE 1]`
**Enforce guardrails structurally:** put the rule in the output contract or format, not only in the role text. `[MODULE 1 – reusable prompt asset]`
An underspecified guardrail is worse than a missing one, because it looks like a control without being one. `[MODULE 1]`
The system prompt shapes behaviour but **isn't enforcement**; pair it with runtime controls. `[MODULE 3]`
sections.Why it matters: A vague prompt is paid for in every request that needs correcting or retrying. Templates concentrate the complexity where it can be reviewed and governed. `[MODULE 1]`
sections.Architecture concepts: Prompt asset versioning; slot validation; output schema; runtime screening and authorization behind the prompt (5.1).
sections.How it works:
1. Write role and scope (in and out of bounds).
2. List must and must-not constraints.
3. Define the exact output contract.
4. Make the safety rules part of the format (e.g. no field exists in which to promise a refund).
5. Parameterise only the variable content.
6. Diagnose gaps: for each requirement, is it *stated* or only *hoped for*?
7. Version and govern the template.
sections.Decision framework:
| Put it in the prompt when… | Put it in runtime controls when… |
|---|---|
| Steering tone, scope, format | It must hold against adversarial input, or the action has side effects |
| Both, for anything high-stakes | |
sections.Exam decision signals:
- "Outputs vary in format across requests" → **output contract missing**.
- "Agent sometimes promises refunds" → **structural guardrail + output screening**.
- "Each team pastes its own version" → **template / Skill governance** (2.5).
sections.Common traps:
- COMMON TRAP: guardrails stated only in prose.
- COMMON TRAP: letting slots override scaffolding.
- COMMON TRAP: assuming the system prompt is a security boundary.
sections.Must remember:
- Role · Scope · Constraints · Output contract.
- Safe path = default path.
- Make the implicit explicit.
- Prompt ≠ enforcement.
sections.Quick recall:
**"Scope it · Format it · Bound it · Version it."**

**Sources:** M1 Prompting as Architecture, reusable prompt asset exercise; M3 Alignment layers.

objectives.official_wording: Apply prompt engineering techniques (zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought)
objectives.module_reference: M1 Prompt engineering techniques across models, Try prompting before fine-tuning, four properties (steerability).

sections.What you need to know:
| Technique | What | When | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Zero-shot** | Instruction only | Well-specified tasks the model handles reliably; **try first** | `[MODULE 1]` |
| **Few-shot** | A handful of input/output examples | Format or judgement easier to *show* than describe | `[MODULE 1]` |
| **Chain-of-thought** | Reason step by step before answering | Multi-step reasoning, logic, when the path matters | `[MODULE 1]` |
Progress deliberately: start zero-shot, add examples only if needed, add reasoning only if the task's structure demands it. Each step adds tokens and latency. `[MODULE 1]`

**Across models:** more capable models need less scaffolding. Re-tune when you change models; the prompt and model are shipped as a pair. `[MODULE 1]`

**Bias:** leading phrasing and unbalanced few-shot sets steer outputs. Phrase neutrally and balance examples. `[MODULE 1]`

**Prompting before fine-tuning:** prompt → tools or retrieval → stronger pattern → fine-tune (rarely; access is limited). `[MODULE 1]`
sections.Why it matters: Heavier techniques are a recurring tax on every call. Stale few-shot examples quietly steer the model wrong. `[MODULE 1]`
sections.Architecture concepts: Example sets as maintained content (versioned, reviewed for balance); per-technique evals.
sections.How it works:
1. Write a clear zero-shot instruction and eval it.
2. If format or judgement fails, add balanced examples covering the real cases.
3. If multi-step reasoning fails, add step-by-step reasoning (or adaptive thinking, 2.1).
4. Re-measure cost and latency.
5. Refresh examples as the task evolves.
sections.Architecture example: REAL-WORLD EXAMPLE – Ticket classification into 12 categories: zero-shot confused two similar categories. Adding 2 balanced examples per confusable category fixed it. Chain-of-thought added latency with no gain, so it was not used. `[INFERENCE – applies M1 progression]`
sections.Decision framework:
| Use few-shot when… | Use CoT when… |
|---|---|
| Output style or label boundary is hard to describe | Correctness depends on intermediate reasoning |
| **Avoid** unbalanced or stale examples | **Avoid** on simple classification (cost with no gain) |
sections.Exam decision signals:
- "Format inconsistent though instructions are clear" → **few-shot**.
- "Arithmetic or multi-step logic errors" → **CoT** (or code execution for precision `[MODULE 1]`).
- "Outputs skew toward one class" → **check example balance and phrasing**.
sections.Common traps:
- COMMON TRAP: CoT everywhere.
- COMMON TRAP: few-shot sets that show only happy cases.
- COMMON TRAP: fine-tuning first.
- COMMON TRAP: using CoT where deterministic computation should own the answer.
sections.Must remember:
- Zero → few → CoT, only as needed.
- Show rather than tell for format.
- Balance examples.
- Re-tune per model.
sections.Quick recall:
**"Tell · then Show · then Think."**

**Sources:** M1 Prompt engineering techniques across models, Try prompting before fine-tuning, four properties (steerability).

objectives.official_wording: Optimize context windows and manage token usage
objectives.module_reference: M1 How Claude Behaves (working memory), Model & Context Strategy (terms, sizing); M2 Sizing.

sections.What you need to know:
**Working memory is a hard edge.** Content outside the window doesn't exist for the model. Two distinct errors `[MODULE 1]`:
- **Oversized request** (rejected before generation): `400 invalid_request_error` ("prompt is too long", token limit) or `413 request_too_large` (byte limit).
- **Generation hits the ceiling:** stop reason `model_context_window_exceeded`, with truncated output.

**Measure, don't estimate:** read the response's `usage` field and use the **token-counting API** before sending. Characters-per-token ratios are rough. `[MODULE 1]`

**Budget below the ceiling:** largest realistic conversation + retrieved context + system prompt + working scratch + margin. *The window is a ceiling, not a target.* `[MODULE 1]`

**Separate the terms** `[MODULE 1]`:
- **context window** = active attention, reset between calls;
- **retrieval** = fetched knowledge;
- **persistent application state** = owned by your system, needs a tool call;
- **summaries / memory** = continuity managed by the application.

**Token distributions are skewed;** model the tail. `[MODULE 2]`
Attention quality can degrade on very long contexts before the hard limit. `[MODULE 1]`
Strategy (progressive vs. monolithic, 3.8) and **sizing** are separate decisions. `[MODULE 1]`
sections.Why it matters: Both the limit and the bill are per token. A conversation that starts at 4k tokens can be carrying 80k by turn 30. `[MODULE 1]`
sections.Architecture concepts: Token budget per component; front-load critical information; summarise across turns; check the usage field on every response; chunk inputs that exceed the window. `[MODULE 1]` `[MODULE 2]`
sections.How it works:
1. Count tokens for each component (system, history, retrieval, tools, output).
2. Model the p95 conversation, not the average.
3. Set a budget with margin.
4. Choose a strategy to stay under it (progressive, retrieval, compaction).
5. Handle 400/413 before sending and `model_context_window_exceeded` after.
6. Monitor usage in production.
sections.Architecture example: REAL-WORLD EXAMPLE – A long legal chat began returning truncated answers late in sessions (`model_context_window_exceeded`). Fix: compact earlier turns into a decision summary (keeping clause IDs verbatim), retrieve clauses just in time, and keep the stable policy as a cached prefix. `[INFERENCE – applies M1]`
sections.Decision framework:
| Symptom | Cause | Response |
|---|---|---|
| 400 prompt too long | Request over the token limit | Trim, chunk, retrieve instead |
| 413 | Body over the byte limit | Reduce payload (e.g. attachments) |
| Truncated output, context-window stop reason | Generation hit the ceiling | Reduce input / compact; raise output headroom |
| Cost growing per turn | Accumulation | Progressive + compaction |
sections.Exam decision signals:
- "Fits, but output stops early" → **context-window stop reason**, not a 400.
- "Estimated tokens by characters" → **use token counting / usage**.
- "Designed to the full window" → **no margin**.
sections.Common traps:
- COMMON TRAP: confusing an oversized request with a mid-generation ceiling.
- COMMON TRAP: designing to the ceiling.
- COMMON TRAP: assuming the model remembers prior calls.
sections.Must remember:
- 400/413 = rejected before generation; `model_context_window_exceeded` = stopped during it.
- Usage field + token counting.
- Budget with margin.
- Memory is application-managed.
sections.Quick recall:
**"Count it · Budget it · Leave room."**

**Sources:** M1 How Claude Behaves (working memory), Model & Context Strategy (terms, sizing); M2 Sizing.

objectives.official_wording: Implement prompt reuse strategies (caching, modular prompts, Skills)
objectives.module_reference: M1 Caching mechanics, modular prompts and Skills; Skills as an integration mechanism; M2 Sizing (caching); M5 Skills distribution; Official – Agent Skills.

sections.What you need to know:
**Prompt caching** reuses a stable prefix `[MODULE 1]` `[MODULE 2]`:
- **Cache breakpoints:** mark where the fixed part ends.
- **Ordering:** static before dynamic, always.
- **TTL:** match it to how often content changes and how often it's called (default 5 minutes `[MODULE 2]`).
- **Write overhead:** writes cost more than standard input. For rarely called or small prefixes, caching can cost more than it saves.
- Needs explicit `cache_control` markers. `[MODULE 2]`
- The response is identical with or without caching. `[MODULE 2]`
- If cached content must reflect live state, caching opens a consistency window. `[MODULE 2]`

**Modular prompt library vs. Skill** `[MODULE 1]`:
| Lean toward library | Lean toward Skill |
|---|---|
| Assembled and tweaked per use | A stable procedure run the same way every time |
| Shared within one codebase or team | Distributed across teams or products |
| Lightweight governance | Needs versioning, approval, rollback |

**A Skill** is a SKILL.md with instructions, optional scripts and version management, travelling as one governed unit. On the API it's attached via `container.skills`, published and versioned via `/v1/skills`, and **requires the Code Execution Tool** (a sandboxed execution dependency). `[MODULE 1]`
**Team distribution:** org-provisioned, plugin assigned to a group (strongest governance + rollback), Claude Code project Skills (`.claude/skills/`, versioned with the repo), API Skills (version pinning). `[MODULE 5]`
Skills load **progressively**: metadata first, content on demand. `[OFFICIAL ANTHROPIC DOCS – Agent Skills]`
sections.Why it matters: A cache that never hits: one team put the per-request document *before* the fixed instructions, and the prefix changed on every call. Ungoverned prompts copied across teams drift into many versions. `[MODULE 1]`
sections.Architecture concepts: Prefix design; versioned prompt assets; Skill registry with a trusted-source policy and audit (5.1); rollback path.
sections.How it works:
1. Separate static from dynamic content.
2. Order static first; place the breakpoint.
3. Model cache economics (frequency, prefix size, write cost, TTL).
4. Decide library vs. Skill by repeatability, distribution and governance.
5. Package stable procedures as versioned Skills; choose a distribution mechanism (7.1).
6. Audit third-party Skills before use.
sections.Decision framework:
| Use caching when… | Skip caching when… |
|---|---|
| Long, stable prefix; frequent calls within the TTL | Rare calls; small prefix; content must be live |
| **Use Skill** for repeatable, distributed, governed procedures | **Use library** for flexible, team-local assembly |
sections.Exam decision signals:
- "Caching enabled, no savings" → **dynamic content before the breakpoint** / low frequency.
- "Same procedure across many teams, needs rollback" → **Skill (via plugin)**.
- "8k identical prefix each call" → **cache** (EG Sample 2).
sections.Common traps:
- COMMON TRAP: caching everything.
- COMMON TRAP: forgetting the Code Execution Tool dependency of API Skills.
- COMMON TRAP: copy-paste reuse with no versioning.
sections.Must remember:
- Static first · breakpoint · TTL · write cost.
- Library = flexible; Skill = governed.
- Skills load progressively.
- Version everything you share.
sections.Quick recall:
**"Fixed first, cache it; repeat often, Skill it; share widely, version it."**

**Sources:** M1 Caching mechanics, modular prompts and Skills; Skills as an integration mechanism; M2 Sizing (caching); M5 Skills distribution; Official – Agent Skills.

objectives.official_wording: Evaluate tool/agent configuration for capability bloat
objectives.module_reference: M2 Least-privilege tool configuration; M1 Pattern Selection; EG Sample 1; Official docs – tool search tool.
source_labels: OFFICIAL ANTHROPIC DOCS – tool search tool

sections.What you need to know:
Every tool you connect to Claude is both an **attack surface and a cost**. For each tool, ask whether it is *essential* to the task or merely *convenient*. Remove anything out of scope and record why. In orchestrator-worker systems, scope each subagent's tools to its own task so it cannot reach tools its job doesn't need. `[MODULE 2 – Least-privilege tool configuration]`
An agent "can do anything its tools allow, including combinations you didn't test for", so the tool surface should be as narrow as the task allows. `[MODULE 1 – Pattern Selection, Cost·Complexity·Risk]`
"Capability bloat" is the exam's name for this problem; the modules describe it as excess tools or permissions. `[INFERENCE]`
sections.Why it matters: Least privilege removes risk at the source. Logging, confirmation prompts and bigger models only *compensate* for risk that is still there. A bloated tool set also uses context tokens on every call and makes it harder for the model to pick the right tool. `[EXAM GUIDE – Sample 1 rationale]` `[INFERENCE]`
sections.Architecture concepts:
- **Components:** tool definitions, the agent/subagent configuration, and the authorization layer.
- **Pattern:** least-privilege tool configuration plus a trust hierarchy (orchestrator → scoped subagents). `[MODULE 2]`
- **Security:** an unused side-effecting tool (refund, delete, send) is pure liability. `[EXAM GUIDE Sample 1]`
- **Lifecycle:** re-audit tool sets when the role or task changes. Record why each tool was removed. `[MODULE 2]`
- **Related:** deferred tool loading (3.8) reduces *context* cost for large catalogues, but does **not** reduce *permissions*. `[OFFICIAL ANTHROPIC DOCS – tool search tool]` `[INFERENCE]`
sections.How it works:
1. List every tool and permission available to each agent or subagent.
2. Map each one to a task the role actually performs.
3. Classify each as essential, convenient or out of scope.
4. Remove the out-of-scope ones entirely and write down why.
5. Scope each subagent to its own task (read-only where possible).
6. Put deterministic authorization in front of whatever side-effecting tools remain (5.1).
sections.Architecture example: REAL-WORLD EXAMPLE – A support agent has `read_ticket`, `draft_reply`, `issue_refund` and `delete_account`. Support staff only read and draft. The right change is to **remove** `issue_refund` and `delete_account` from that agent. Refunds go to a separate, human-approved workflow. `[EXAM GUIDE Sample 1]`
sections.Decision framework:
| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| When to use | Always: during design review, before production, and whenever a role changes |
| When NOT to strip tools | When the task genuinely needs the capability. Then keep it and add deterministic authorization plus a HITL gate |
| Alternatives | Authorization gate (still needed for kept tools); confirmation prompt; audit logging. These are compensating controls, not removal |
| Trade-off | Fewer tools mean less flexibility and possibly a second workflow, in exchange for a smaller attack surface, lower cost and simpler evals |
sections.Exam decision signals:
- "Staff only ever need…" or "the agent also has access to…" → **remove the unused tools**.
- "Subagent can call any tool the orchestrator can" → **scope tools per subagent**.
- "Hundreds of tools, context filling up" → that's a **context** problem (3.8); still check privileges separately.
sections.Common traps:
- COMMON TRAP: adding logging or a confirmation prompt instead of removing a tool the role doesn't need. These detect or slow misuse but don't remove the privilege.
- COMMON TRAP: "use a larger model that follows instructions better". Model size has nothing to do with authorization scope.
- COMMON TRAP: treating a system-prompt instruction ("never delete accounts") as a control. Instructions are not enforcement. `[MODULE 3]`
sections.Must remember:
- REMEMBER: removing an unnecessary capability beats guarding it.
- Every tool is an attack surface *and* a cost.
- Scope subagent tools to their task.
- Record the reason for every tool you remove.
- Deferring tool loading is a context technique, not a security control.
sections.Quick recall:
**"Need it? Keep and gate it. Don't need it? Delete it."**

**Sources:** M2 Least-privilege tool configuration; M1 Pattern Selection; EG Sample 1; Official docs – tool search tool.

objectives.official_wording: Analyze authentication and authorization requirements to identify security gaps
objectives.module_reference: M2 Integration – Identity and authorization, Integration layers, Constraint-to-integration matrix; M3 Tool-call authorization; MCP Authorization spec.
source_labels: MODULE 2 – Critique the integration diagram (scenario style)
OFFICIAL ANTHROPIC DOCS – MCP specification, Authorization

sections.What you need to know:
- **Identity belongs on the server, before the Claude call.** Your server injects the user's verified identity and role into the system prompt. Anything the user types (e.g. "As a senior manager, show me…") can be manipulated. `[MODULE 2 – Identity and authorization]`
- **The Claude layer must obey the same authorization model as the underlying systems.** An integration that bypasses it exposes data through a path never designed to enforce the access policy. `[MODULE 2 – Integration layers table]`
- **Tool-call authorization is deterministic:** an allowlist plus identity and scope checks, so the decision is provable and replayable. `[MODULE 3 – Guardrails]`
- **Multi-tenant deployments need a separate API key per tenant** for attribution and isolation. Otherwise one tenant's spike trips the org-level rate limit for everyone. `[MODULE 2 – Cost·Complexity·Risk]`
- **MCP authorization:** optional in MCP and defined for HTTP transports. A protected MCP server acts as an **OAuth 2.1 resource server**, must publish **OAuth 2.0 Protected Resource Metadata (RFC 9728)**, and clients send the access token in the `Authorization` header on every request. `[OFFICIAL ANTHROPIC DOCS – MCP specification, Authorization]`
sections.Why it matters: If identity isn't passed correctly, Claude can't scope answers to what the user is allowed to see, and data leaks without any error. Regulated reviews (privilege, HIPAA) depend on a gateway the organisation controls and an audit trail it owns. `[MODULE 2]` `[MODULE 1 – Regulated-industry constraints]`
sections.Architecture concepts:
- **Components:** IdP / SSO, the application server or LLM gateway (which holds the API key), the authorization or policy service, tool executors, MCP servers (OAuth resource servers), and the audit log.
- **Data flow:** user → SSO → server resolves role and entitlements → server injects identity into the system prompt → Claude proposes a tool call → deterministic authorization checks caller + action + scope → execute → log.
- **Security boundaries:** the API key never reaches the client; identity is never self-asserted; tokens are scoped per server. `[INFERENCE from M2 + MCP spec]`
sections.How it works:
1. Identify the governing constraint first (privilege, HIPAA, residency); it may remove some entry points. `[MODULE 2]`
2. Authenticate through the enterprise IdP (SSO).
3. Resolve role and data entitlements on the server.
4. Inject only the minimum identity context Claude needs (role and authorised scope).
5. Run every side-effecting tool call through a deterministic allowlist plus scope check.
6. For remote MCP servers, use OAuth 2.1 and tokens scoped to that server.
7. Use one API key per tenant; log identity, model version and data scope on each request.
sections.Architecture example: REAL-WORLD EXAMPLE – A multi-tenant SaaS support agent was found with: (a) the user's role taken from a chat field, (b) one shared API key for all tenants, (c) a CRM tool that queries any tenant's records. The fixes: role injected server-side from SSO; one API key per tenant; the CRM tool scoped to the authenticated tenant ID by the authorization layer rather than by the prompt. `[MODULE 2 – Critique the integration diagram (scenario style)]` `[INFERENCE]`
sections.Decision framework:
| Situation | Use | Avoid |
|---|---|---|
| User role affects what data Claude may see | Server-side identity injection | Role stated in the user message |
| Side-effecting tool | Deterministic allowlist + identity + scope | Model-based "judgement" of permission |
| Remote MCP server with non-public data | OAuth 2.1 resource-server pattern | Static shared secrets in config |
| Multi-tenant | One API key per tenant | One shared org key |
| Privileged or regulated content | API/SDK behind an org-owned gateway with SSO and logs | Consumer chat tiers |
sections.Exam decision signals:
- "User states their role / department in the prompt" → **identity spoofing gap**; inject server-side.
- "Rate-limit breach, can't tell which customer" → **per-tenant API keys**.
- "Claude can see records the user can't" → **authorization bypass**; enforce the existing policy model.
- "Remote MCP server, enterprise data" → **OAuth 2.1 / RFC 9728**.
sections.Common traps:
- COMMON TRAP: telling Claude in the system prompt to "only show the user's own data". That's an instruction, not authorization.
- COMMON TRAP: treating authentication (who you are) as authorization (what you may do).
- COMMON TRAP: relying on output screening to catch unauthorised actions. Output screening judges text, not actions. `[MODULE 3]`
sections.Must remember:
- Identity is injected by the server, never claimed by the user.
- The Claude layer inherits the existing authorization model; it doesn't bypass it.
- Tool authorization is deterministic and auditable.
- Use one API key per tenant.
- An MCP server is an OAuth 2.1 resource server (RFC 9728 metadata).
sections.Quick recall:
**"Who (SSO) → What role (server) → What action (allowlist) → Logged."**

**Sources:** M2 Integration – Identity and authorization, Integration layers, Constraint-to-integration matrix; M3 Tool-call authorization; MCP Authorization spec.

objectives.official_wording: Evaluate accuracy-latency trade-offs and justify configuration decisions
objectives.module_reference: M1 Model & Context Strategy, extended thinking, Opus 7× case, Calculator; M2 POC to Prod, p95, Calculator.

sections.What you need to know:
The main configuration levers and their effects:
- **Model tier:** Sonnet is the default. Move up to Opus only if an eval shows Sonnet misses the quality bar; move down to Haiku only if an eval confirms the quality loss is acceptable. `[MODULE 1]`
- **Extended / adaptive thinking:** thinking tokens are billed as output and add latency. Turn it on only for a measured accuracy gap after prompt work. `[MODULE 1]`
- **Context strategy and size:** cost and latency grow linearly with input length. `[MODULE 1]`
- **Retrieval design:** smaller chunks and hybrid indexes raise quality *and* latency. `[MODULE 1 – RAG]`
- **`max_tokens` cap, caching, Batch API** (when the SLA allows async processing). `[MODULE 2]`

Design against **p95, not the median**. SLA breaches come from the slow tail. `[MODULE 2]`
When cost and latency budgets both apply, **name the binding constraint**: if latency is binding, tier and thinking are the main controls; if cost is binding, tier and context strategy are. `[MODULE 1 – Calculator model answer]`
sections.Why it matters: Defaulting to "the best model" with thinking turned on everywhere caused a 7× cost overrun and 2.3 s median latency against an 800 ms target, with no gain in customer satisfaction. Routing each step to a tier based on evals cut cost by 71%. `[MODULE 1 – Opus-everywhere case]`
sections.Architecture concepts:
- Per-step model routing (classifier → Haiku, summarisation → Sonnet, final composition → Opus, each only if the eval supports it).
- Eval set + pre-set rollback threshold as the justification artefact.
- Latency budget (p95) and cost ceiling as twin constraints.
sections.How it works:
1. State the accuracy threshold, p95 latency target and cost ceiling (the numbers come from the business).
2. Build an eval set that covers each pipeline step.
3. Run a baseline (Sonnet, no thinking, progressive context).
4. Change **one lever at a time**; measure accuracy, p95 and cost.
5. Identify the binding constraint and the lever that moves it.
6. Document the configuration, the rejected alternatives and the rollback criterion.
sections.Architecture example: REAL-WORLD EXAMPLE – A routing classifier had extended thinking turned on. The eval showed no accuracy gain, but p95 rose a lot. The fix: thinking off and the classifier moved to Haiku (no regression on the eval). The higher tier stays only on the final response step, where the eval says it earns its place. `[MODULE 1]`
sections.Decision framework:
| Lever | Raises accuracy when… | Costs | Don't use when… |
|---|---|---|---|
| Higher tier | Eval shows a quality gap | Cost and latency | Simple classification or extraction already passes |
| Thinking | Multi-step reasoning gap after prompt work | Output tokens and latency | Routing or classification steps |
| Bigger context | Task needs all the material at once | Linear cost and latency; attention degrades | Long multi-turn loops |
| Hybrid retrieval / small chunks | Exact-match queries are being missed | Latency and compute | Pure paraphrase queries |
sections.Exam decision signals:
- "Latency target missed, accuracy fine" → lower the tier or turn off thinking on that step.
- "Used the best model to be safe" → **per-step tiering justified by evals**.
- "Median is fine, users complain" → look at **p95**.
sections.Common traps:
- COMMON TRAP: "turn on thinking, it can't hurt". It costs tokens and latency on every call.
- COMMON TRAP: one model for every step.
- COMMON TRAP: justifying a configuration from a demo rather than an eval.
- COMMON TRAP: optimising average latency instead of p95.
sections.Must remember:
- Sonnet first; moving tier is a measured decision.
- Thinking is a cost/latency trade-off; turn it on only when an eval shows it helps.
- p95 is the design target.
- Name the binding constraint and its main lever.
- Not choosing a model means choosing the most expensive one.
sections.Quick recall:
**"Measure → one lever → re-measure → justify."**

**Sources:** M1 Model & Context Strategy, extended thinking, Opus 7× case, Calculator; M2 POC to Prod, p95, Calculator.

objectives.official_wording: Analyze observability challenges and select monitoring strategies at scale
objectives.module_reference: M2 Integration – Observability; M2 A/B & Obs – Observability at scale; M1 Multi-agent failure table.

sections.What you need to know:
LLM systems rarely crash. They produce responses that are **subtly wrong**, so standard error logging misses most failures. `[MODULE 2]`
**Log four things per request:**
- the request: model version, input tokens, prompt ID;
- the response: output tokens, latency, stop reason;
- the context: user role, session ID, whether the cache was hit;
- the outcome: accepted or rejected downstream. `[MODULE 2]`

**Monitor in four layers** `[MODULE 2 – Observability at scale]`:
1. **Request-level tracing**, including tool calls.
2. **Metric aggregation:** cost per request, p50/p95, task success, errors by type. Break metrics down per request, because averages hide expensive tails.
3. **Anomaly detection:** e.g. cost above 150% of the 7-day average, p95 above SLA. Gradual drift needs periodic comparison of output distributions.
4. **Change attribution:** model drift vs. data drift vs. model-update effect. Each has a different fix.

Multi-agent systems need a **shared trace ID** across the orchestrator and subagents. `[MODULE 1]`
Check which agent actions each surface writes to its audit log. An action that isn't logged can't be approved by a security reviewer. `[MODULE 2]`
sections.Why it matters: Observability is a prerequisite for letting agents act at all. Adding it after an incident means rebuilding the root cause from data that can't answer the question. `[MODULE 2]`
sections.Architecture concepts: Trace pipeline → metrics store → dashboards and alerts → attribution analysis → a translation layer to business KPIs (e.g. task success → first-contact resolution). `[MODULE 2]` Lifecycle: build it at design time.
sections.How it works:
1. List the questions you'll need to answer after an incident.
2. Instrument request, response, context and outcome on every call.
3. Propagate a trace ID across agents and tools.
4. Aggregate per request and per segment, not only overall.
5. Set threshold alerts plus periodic distribution checks for drift.
6. Pin model versions so you can attribute changes. `[MODULE 2 – Model version pinning]`
7. Map technical metrics to the sponsor's KPIs.
sections.Architecture example: REAL-WORLD EXAMPLE – Dashboards were green while a small share of very long documents used most of the budget and produced wrong outputs. Per-request breakdown by input-length bucket exposed it; aggregate metrics never would have. `[MODULE 2]`
sections.Decision framework:
| Need | Strategy |
|---|---|
| Hard failures (errors, timeouts) | Threshold alerts |
| Slow quality erosion | Periodic eval or distribution comparison; trigger in the feedback loop (6.3) |
| "Why did cost jump?" | Per-request decomposition: tier, cache hits, token counts |
| Multi-agent debugging | Shared trace ID, subagent coverage checks |
| Exec reporting | KPI translation layer |
Trade-off: richer logs add storage and sensitive-data exposure (minimise PII, 5.4).
sections.Exam decision signals:
- "No errors but users say answers are worse" → drift detection and attribution.
- "Can't reconstruct which step approved X" → trace and audit logging.
- "Aggregate looks fine" → per-request decomposition.
sections.Common traps:
- COMMON TRAP: relying on error rate to catch LLM quality issues.
- COMMON TRAP: mixing up model drift, data drift and a model-version update.
- COMMON TRAP: logging raw PII "for observability".
sections.Must remember:
- LLMs fail quietly; instrument the outcome.
- Log request, response, context and outcome.
- Decompose per request; averages lie.
- Attribute changes before you fix them.
- Shared trace ID across agents.
sections.Quick recall:
**"Trace → Aggregate → Alert → Attribute → Translate."**

**Sources:** M2 Integration – Observability; M2 A/B & Obs – Observability at scale; M1 Multi-agent failure table.

objectives.official_wording: Design a RAG pipeline with appropriate chunking and indexing strategies
objectives.module_reference: M1 RAG Pipeline Design; M2 Failure modes (RAG); EG Sample 3.

sections.What you need to know:
Choose the **chunking** strategy from the *structure of the source*, and the **index** from *how users phrase queries*. `[MODULE 1 – RAG Pipeline Design]`

| Chunking | Use when |
|---|---|
| Fixed-size (with overlap) | Homogeneous, unstructured text; simplest to run |
| Semantic | Prose where each chunk must stand alone |
| Hierarchical | Contracts, manuals, policies where section context carries meaning |

| Index | Matches | Use when |
|---|---|---|
| Dense (embeddings) | Meaning | Queries are paraphrased |
| Sparse (BM25, keyword) | Exact tokens | Part numbers, statute citations, error codes |
| Hybrid + **Reciprocal Rank Fusion** | Both | Mixed query patterns (the common production case) |

Every design trades **retrieval quality vs. latency vs. maintenance**. `[MODULE 1]`
sections.Why it matters: Retrieval quality is invisible in the output. A confident answer built on the wrong chunk looks the same as a correct one, so you have to measure retrieval against a labelled set. `[MODULE 1]`
sections.Architecture concepts:
Ingestion → parsing (OCR where needed) → chunking → embedding / sparse indexing → retrieval → (fusion) → context assembly → generation with citations → eval loop on retrieval precision/recall. `[MODULE 1]` `[MODULE 2 – RAG failure modes]`
Lifecycle: re-index when documents change; keep embeddings matched to the query encoder. `[EXAM GUIDE Sample 3]`
sections.How it works:
1. Characterise the corpus: structure, size, how often it changes.
2. Characterise queries: paraphrase vs. exact identifiers.
3. Pick the chunking strategy (respect tables, code blocks and section boundaries).
4. Pick dense, sparse or hybrid; fuse with RRF if hybrid.
5. Build a labelled retrieval eval set; measure precision and recall.
6. Set a refresh / re-index schedule and monitor retrieval drift.
sections.Architecture example: REAL-WORLD EXAMPLE – A regulatory Q&A system over statutes. Queries cite section numbers ("§ 4.2(b)") and also ask conceptual questions. Use hierarchical chunking by section, a hybrid index (BM25 for citations plus embeddings for concepts) and RRF. Precision on the citation-heavy part of the eval jumped once sparse retrieval was added. `[INFERENCE – applies M1 rules]`
sections.Decision framework:
| Use A when… | Use B when… |
|---|---|
| **Dense**: paraphrase/intent queries | **Sparse**: identifier/code queries |
| **Small chunks**: precise facts | **Larger / hierarchical chunks**: context-heavy reasoning |
| Avoid dense-only when exact matches matter. Avoid tiny chunks that split tables or arguments. | |
sections.Exam decision signals:
- "Misses part numbers / error codes" → **add sparse (hybrid)**.
- "Answers lose clause context" → **hierarchical chunking**.
- "Wrong after a document refresh" → **re-indexing / embedding mismatch** (EG Sample 3).
sections.Common traps:
- COMMON TRAP: one default chunk size for every corpus.
- COMMON TRAP: fixing a retrieval problem by switching to a bigger model.
- COMMON TRAP: judging RAG only on final-answer quality, without retrieval metrics.
sections.Must remember:
- Chunk by structure; index by query pattern.
- Hybrid + RRF is the safe default for mixed queries.
- Measure retrieval separately from generation.

objectives.official_wording: Apply retrieval strategies matched to data shape and query pattern
objectives.module_reference: M1 Reference Architectures, "When retrieval got reached for instead of a tool call", Model & Context – distinct terms.

sections.What you need to know:
**Retrieval is for stable knowledge. Tool calls are for live state.** `[MODULE 1]`
- **Stable knowledge** (FAQs, policies, manuals) changes slower than your index refresh → **RAG**.
- **Live state** (order status, inventory, balances) is owned by a system of record → **a tool or API call**.
- **Persistent application state** belongs to your system, not the model → tool call. `[MODULE 1 – Distinct terms]`
- Use **monolithic context** when the material is small and stable; use **retrieval** when the corpus is too large or changes faster than redeployments. `[MODULE 1]`
sections.Why it matters: Retrieval applied to live state returns confident, fluent, wrong answers with normal latency and no errors. "Similarity is not truth." `[MODULE 1 – electronics retailer trace]`
sections.Architecture concepts: Context engineering means deciding *which mechanism owns getting each kind of data in front of the model*. Typical layout: an intent router → knowledge retrieval (docs) / transactional API (live state) / human approval (high-consequence). `[MODULE 1 – Customer-service reference architecture]`
sections.How it works:
1. Classify each data type: stable reference, live transactional, user/session state, or computed values.
2. Stable → retrieval; live → tool call to the system of record; computed precision → code execution or deterministic service.
3. Route by intent.
4. Keep live-state queries out of the index entirely.
5. Evaluate each path with its own eval set. `[MODULE 1 – separate eval contract per architecture]`
sections.Architecture example: REAL-WORLD EXAMPLE – "Where's my order?" pulled two stale chunks (similarity 0.78 and 0.74) and answered "shipped on the 12th". The order had actually been returned to the depot. The fix was not a better chunker or a shorter refresh interval. It was **calling the order-status API**, which already existed. `[MODULE 1]`
sections.Decision framework:
| Data | Mechanism | Avoid |
|---|---|---|
| Manual / policy | RAG (with citations) | Fine-tuning it into the model |
| Order / inventory / price | Tool call to the system of record | Indexing snapshots |
| Arithmetic / exact totals | Code execution / deterministic service | Model mental math |
| Small, stable, always-needed | Monolithic prefix + caching | Retrieval overhead |
sections.Exam decision signals:
- "Answer contradicts the database" / "changes with each index refresh" → **use a tool call, not RAG**.
- "Needs source citations, large corpus" → **RAG**.
- "Tiny stable policy in every request" → **cache the prefix**, no retrieval.
sections.Common traps:
- COMMON TRAP: shortening the re-index interval to "fix" live-state staleness.
- COMMON TRAP: raising the similarity threshold.
- COMMON TRAP: reusing RAG because "it worked on the last project".
sections.Must remember:
- Retrieval = knowledge; tools = state.
- Similarity ≠ truth.
- A stale but confident answer gives no error signal.
- Separate evals per mechanism.
sections.Quick recall:
**"Was true yesterday and will be tomorrow → retrieve. Changes on its own → call the owner."**

**Sources:** M1 Reference Architectures, "When retrieval got reached for instead of a tool call", Model & Context – distinct terms.

sections.What you need to know:
| Mechanism | What it is | Pick it when |
|---|---|---|
| **Direct API** | HTTP Messages API; the foundation layer | You need full control, or the SDK doesn't expose a new feature yet `[MODULE 1]` |
| **SDK** (Python, TS, Java, Go, Ruby, C#, PHP) | Same capability with language-native types, retries and streaming helpers | Default for embedding Claude in a product `[MODULE 1]` |
| **MCP** | Open protocol for *sharing* tools, prompts and resources across clients | The **same** tool surface must be reachable from **two or more** Claude clients `[MODULE 1]` |
| **Agent SDK** | Managed agent loop (the same one that powers Claude Code), embedded in your app | Claude must act over multiple turns inside *your* product `[MODULE 1, 2]` |
| **Claude Code (CLI/IDE)** | Agentic coding tool | The user is a developer doing engineering work; not a backend for multi-tenant products `[MODULE 2]` |
| **Agent-to-agent** | Delegation between independently owned agents | Source gap – see below |

**MCP vs. API tool use** are different layers, not alternatives: an MCP server exposes tools that clients call through API tool use. `[MODULE 1]`
**Agent-to-agent:** Anthropic's own multi-agent research system uses an orchestrator-worker design with parallel subagents, which costs about 15× the tokens of chat and suits poorly when agents need shared context or have many dependencies. `[OFFICIAL ANTHROPIC DOCS – multi-agent research system]` The A2A protocol is an open protocol announced by Google and positioned as complementary to MCP (external source, not Anthropic). Source gap – verification required: no official Anthropic guidance on agent-to-agent protocols was found.
sections.Why it matters: The most common integration mistakes are reaching for Claude Code for non-engineering work and treating MCP as the default integration layer whether or not its reuse is needed. `[MODULE 1]`
sections.Architecture concepts: Three layers that must not be collapsed: **entry point** (chosen for the user), **build-time interface** (chosen for the engineering team), **delivery route** (chosen for cloud commitments and compliance). `[MODULE 1 – Platform Map]` Each integration boundary has its own auth, logging and failure profile. `[MODULE 4]`
sections.How it works:
1. Name the user and the work (this decides the entry point).
2. Let compliance eliminate routes and entry points first.
3. Single request/response → API or SDK.
4. Multi-turn agent inside your product → Agent SDK (or a custom API loop if you need control between turns).
5. Tool surface reused by several clients → MCP.
6. Delegation to agents you don't own or control → evaluate an agent-to-agent protocol `[INFERENCE]`.
7. Document an entry-point-responsibility map. `[MODULE 4]`
sections.Architecture example: REAL-WORLD EXAMPLE – A bank proposed Claude Code on branch laptops with MCP servers and compliance-checking subagents. The right design is a custom web app calling the API with SSO, compliance in deterministic server-side code, and tool calls audited at the server. MCP isn't needed because no other Claude clients reuse the tools. `[MODULE 1]`
sections.Decision framework:
| Use MCP when… | Use direct tool use when… |
|---|---|
| Two or more clients need the same tools | Tools live inside one product |
| **Avoid MCP** when only one client ever uses it (overhead, harder debugging `[MODULE 2]`) | **Avoid** duplicating tool code across clients |
| **Agent SDK** when you want a managed multi-turn loop | **Raw API loop** when you need custom logic between turns |
sections.Exam decision signals:
- "Same tools from Claude.ai, Claude Code and an internal app" → **MCP**.
- "Non-technical staff, operational workflow" → **not Claude Code**; custom app on API/SDK.
- "Agent embedded in our web app acting over several turns" → **Agent SDK**.
- "Partner organisation's agent built on another framework" → **agent-to-agent protocol** `[INFERENCE]`.
sections.Common traps:
- COMMON TRAP: "It's all Claude" – picking an entry point before naming the user.
- COMMON TRAP: MCP by habit.
- COMMON TRAP: confusing the Anthropic SDK (a wrapper) with the Agent SDK (a managed loop).
- COMMON TRAP: putting high-consequence compliance logic in subagents instead of deterministic code.
sections.Must remember:
- API and SDK are the same entry point with different ergonomics.
- MCP = sharing across clients; tool use = calling inside one request.
- Agent SDK = an embedded managed loop.
- Claude Code = developers.
- The entry point follows the user and the work.
sections.Quick recall:
**"One call → API/SDK · Many clients → MCP · Many turns in my app → Agent SDK · Dev work → Claude Code."**
